title: Arterial Line (A-Line) Management & Zeroing
summary: Managing an indwelling arterial catheter for continuous blood pressure monitoring and ABG sampling.
equipment: Pressurized normal saline bag (300 mmHg pressure)
steps: Confirm arterial line placement site (radial most common) and verify Allen's test was performed prior to insertion.
Pressurize the NS bag to 300 mmHg to ensure the continuous flush (3 mL/hr) is active.
ZEROING: Level the transducer to the phlebostatic axis (4th intercostal space, mid-axillary line — right atrium level).
Turn the stopcock off to the patient and open to air. Press 'zero' on the monitor. Wait for confirmation.
Turn stopcock back to patient. Confirm a sharp waveform with systolic peak, dicrotic notch, and diastolic trough.
Compare arterial BP reading to cuff BP upon any concern about accuracy.
Waveform assessment: Over-damped (no dicrotic notch, blunt) — air bubble or clot. Under-damped (exaggerated systolic) — check connections.
Assess insertion site hourly: skin color, sensation, capillary refill of hand/fingers distal to line.
ABG sampling: cleanse stopcock, withdraw waste (1–2 mL), withdraw sample into ABG syringe, flush line, recap.
Document: zeroing time, waveform quality, distal perfusion assessment.
safetyTips: NEVER inject medications or IV fluids through an arterial line — intra-arterial injection can cause permanent limb ischemia.
Label all arterial line tubing RED to prevent wrong-route errors.
Accidental disconnection = massive hemorrhage. Keep connections secure and visible at all times.
keyTakeaways: Level to phlebostatic axis before zeroing
Over-damped = false low; under-damped = false high

title: Temporary Transvenous Pacemaker Management
summary: Monitoring and managing a temporary transvenous cardiac pacemaker.
steps: Confirm pacemaker settings per order: rate (demand pacing: 60–80 bpm), output (mA), sensitivity (mV).
Identify pacemaker spikes on the rhythm strip. Pacing spikes should be followed by capture (P wave for atrial; wide QRS for ventricular).
CAPTURE: Pacemaker spike followed by the appropriate complex = captured. Every spike should capture.
SENSING: Pacemaker should inhibit when patient's own rate is above set rate (demand mode). Failure to sense = competes with native rhythm.
Failure to capture: increase output (mA). Notify provider. Ensure connections are secure.
Failure to sense: adjust sensitivity. Notify provider.
Secure the pulse generator to patient (pinned to gown or bed — never hanging free).
Protect insertion site (subclavian or femoral) — assess for infection, bleeding, dislodgement.
Limit movement of the insertion-side extremity.
Keep rubber gloves at bedside — if generator disconnects, wear gloves before touching bare wire ends (microshock risk).
Document: set rate, output, sensitivity, underlying rhythm, capture and sensing status.
safetyTips: Microshock risk: exposed pacing wires can transmit stray current directly to the myocardium. Wear gloves when handling.
Maintain electrical safety: avoid contact with electrical equipment and patient simultaneously.
Loss of capture in a pacer-dependent patient = emergency. Have atropine and transcutaneous pacing available.
keyTakeaways: Demand mode inhibits when native rate is adequate
Microshock risk — gloves for all wire handling

title: Sequential Compression Device (SCD) Application
summary: Applying and managing sequential compression devices for DVT prophylaxis in hospitalized patients.
steps: Verify order for SCDs and confirm no contraindications: active DVT, acute PE, severe peripheral arterial disease, open wounds on the legs, recent vascular surgery on the extremity.
Assess bilateral lower extremities: skin integrity, pulses, edema, warmth, calf tenderness (Homans' sign — limited specificity).
Select correct sleeve size based on calf circumference (measured at widest point).
Apply sleeves with the tubing connector positioned on the outer aspect of the leg.
Ensure one to two fingers fit between the sleeve and the leg — not too tight, not loose.
Connect tubing to the pump controller. Turn on controller.
Confirm inflation cycle: distal → proximal compression (peristaltic cycle promotes venous return).
Remove sleeves for skin assessment and hygiene at least once per shift. Reassess legs each removal.
Reinforce to patient to keep SCDs on except when ambulating or bathing.
Document: application time, sleeve size and type, bilateral leg assessment findings.
safetyTips: SCDs are contraindicated with known DVT — compression could dislodge a thrombus causing PE.
Remove and assess skin every shift — moisture and pressure under SCDs can cause skin breakdown.
SCDs alone are not sufficient for high-risk patients — ensure pharmacologic prophylaxis is also ordered.
keyTakeaways: Check fit: two fingers between sleeve and leg
Remove each shift for skin assessment

title: Doppler Vascular Assessment (Peripheral Pulses)
summary: Using a hand-held Doppler to assess peripheral pulses when manual palpation is inadequate.
steps: Identify indication: pulses not palpable, post-vascular procedure, concern for arterial compromise.
Perform hand hygiene. Apply conductive gel to Doppler probe tip.
Locate the pulse site:
Dorsalis pedis (DP): top of foot between 1st and 2nd metatarsals.
Posterior tibial (PT): behind medial malleolus.
Radial: radial groove of the wrist.
Popliteal: posterior knee (with slight knee flexion).
Femoral: femoral triangle (NAVEL: nerve-artery-vein-empty-lymphatics; artery is central).
Place probe at 45° angle to the vessel. Move gently until you hear the signal.
Triphasic signal (whoosh-whoosh-whoosh) = normal arterial flow.
Biphasic signal = mildly reduced flow.
Monophasic signal = significantly reduced flow — notify provider.
No signal = emergency — arterial occlusion suspected — notify provider immediately.
Clean gel from skin and probe. Document signal quality and location.
safetyTips: Loss of a previously present Doppler signal after vascular procedure = arterial emergency — notify surgeon immediately.
Comparing bilateral extremities is essential — unilateral absence is more significant than bilateral weak signals.
A pulse oximeter waveform can also confirm distal perfusion when Doppler is unavailable.

title: Central Venous Pressure (CVP) Monitoring
summary: Measuring and interpreting central venous pressure from a central line transducer to assess volume status.
steps: Level the transducer to the phlebostatic axis (4th ICS, mid-axillary line).
Zero the transducer: turn stopcock off to patient, open to air, press zero on monitor.
Position patient supine (or 0–30° elevation consistently — document position used).
Read CVP from the waveform or numeric display. Normal CVP: 2–8 mmHg.
Low CVP (<2 mmHg): suggests hypovolemia — anticipate fluid challenge.
High CVP (>10–12 mmHg): suggests fluid overload, right heart failure, or tamponade.
Assess CVP trend rather than single value — response to fluid bolus is more meaningful.
CVP waveform components: a wave (atrial contraction), c wave (tricuspid closure), v wave (venous filling).
Cannon a-waves: large 'a' waves = AV dissociation (A-fib with CHB, V-pacing) — notify provider.
Document reading, patient position, and clinical correlation.
safetyTips: CVP alone is a poor predictor of fluid responsiveness — use in context with other hemodynamic parameters.
Never use CVP port for blood products or vasopressors without verifying intended lumen.
Air embolism risk with central line: always cap stopcocks, have patient do Valsalva during tubing changes.
keyTakeaways: Level to phlebostatic axis for accurate reading
